questions.questionText: The tone of the elderly master's remark at the end of the passage is best described as
options: gracious and quietly worried about the craft's future
questions.explanation: He does not mind who wears the cloth, which is generous, but wants someone to learn the craft, which shows concern for its continuity.

questions.questionText: The author's treatment of the debate between commuters and officials can best be described as
questions.explanation: The author reports both the commuters' suggestion and the officials' reply without taking sides.

questions.questionText: The author's attitude towards the anganwadi system is best described as
options: appreciative but concerned about the neglect of its workers
questions.explanation: The author credits the centres with achievements and points out the burdens and lack of support on workers.

questions.questionText: The tone of the passage's description of lane-cricket rules is best described as
questions.explanation: The window and electric-wire rules are described with a light, fond touch.

questions.questionText: The tone of the author is best described as
questions.explanation: The author presents both sides and ends by recommending caution until evidence arrives.

questions.questionText: The tone of the volunteer's closing remark is best described as
questions.explanation: He contrasts the salt tasting sweeter to the buyer than to the maker, a wry comment that carries sorrow about unfair earnings.

questions.questionText: The tone of the last sentence of the passage is
questions.explanation: It acknowledges love for the hills but warns that without care it destroys them.

questions.questionText: The author's attitude towards the technology-based schooling of the pandemic is best described as
questions.explanation: The author acknowledges its value in extending reach but also its limits, concluding that technology cannot replace the school.

questions.questionText: The attitude of Murugan towards his profession is best described as

questions.questionText: The tone of the passage towards the scheme is best described as
options: warmly appreciative with a brief note of criticism
questions.explanation: The author describes benefits favourably and mentions a limitation without hostility.

questions.questionText: The tone of the researcher's last remark is best described as
questions.explanation: Calling a language a house to be kept in repair reassures that it is an asset and encourages care.

questions.questionText: The author's concluding stance is best described as
questions.explanation: 'Neither a cure nor a curse' signals an even view.

questions.questionText: The author's attitude towards the economic criticism of the charkha is best described as
questions.explanation: The author presents the criticism and Gandhi's reply, then says 'whatever one thinks of the economics', neutral and even.

questions.questionText: The tone of the volunteer's remark about the small bird is best described as
options: admiring in a purely commercial way

questions.questionText: The author's attitude towards bazaar bargaining is best described as
questions.explanation: The author explains its logic and notes its decline with some sympathy.

questions.questionText: The author's tone towards parents who fear empty time is best described as
questions.explanation: The author acknowledges their fear and then presents experts' reasoning.

questions.questionText: The tone of the economist's closing hope is best described as

questions.questionText: The author's attitude to the single-screen theatre is best described as

questions.questionText: The tone of the guard's closing comment is best described as

questions.questionText: The tone of the author in describing Dr Meena is best described as
questions.explanation: The account is factual but shows respect for her work.

questions.questionText: The tone in the final sentence is best described as

questions.questionText: The tone of the Karnataka farmer's remark is best described as
